clips.title: Concrete Beats Character Every Time
clips.text: Here's the difference that changes everything. saying, say you were late three times this month instead of you are unreliable. The first statement is a fact you can verify on a calendar. The second is a label that cannot be measured. When you point to the specific behavior, the recipient can agree, apologize, and adjust the habit. When you slap a trait on them, they argue about who they are, not what they did. I've seen a manager replace a vague or disorganized with the report Miss the Deadline twice. and the employee fixed the process within a week. Concrete beats character every time.

clips.title: The 48-Hour Rule: Feedback Timing Matters
clips.text: The 48 -hour rule is simple. Feedback older than two days feels like an ambush. After 48 hours the details blur, the emotion cools, and the recipient starts filling the gaps with their own story, usually a defensive one. I learned this the hard way when I waited a week to address a missed deadline. The engineer thought I was holding a grudge, not coaching a habit. When you deliver the observation within the window, the facts are fresh, the intent is clear, and the conversation stays on track. Miss the window and you trade coaching for conflict.

clips.title: Ditch the Feedback Sandwich for Better Results
clips.text: Here's the hard truth. The feedback sandwich does not work. You lay a praise, criticism, praise, hoping the middle lands, but the brain only remembers the bread. Studies show that recipients recall the positive frames and discard the corrective core, so the behavior never shifts. I've watched managers spend 10 minutes wrapping a single point in compliments, only to hear the same mistake repeated next week. The fix is simple. Drop the filler, name the specific action, and state the impact in one clear sentence. When you stop hiding the message inside a snack, the listener can actually chew on it and change.
